## By page

### [Ch 0 — Foundations](../core/ch0-foundations.md) { #page-ch0-foundations }

#### The path of one read { #fig-ch0-storage-path }

*Figure* · in [§0.3 How a computer is wired](../core/ch0-foundations.md#03-how-a-computer-is-wired)

Software on the host turns "part of a file" into a numbered block and a command; firmware in the drive turns that number into a place in the flash. The data then comes back up the same path.

#### The latency ladder, in typical orders of magnitude { #fig-ch0-latency-ladder }

*Figure* · in [§0.5 Latency, throughput and IOPS](../core/ch0-foundations.md#05-latency-throughput-and-iops)

An SSD read is about a thousand times slower than DRAM and about a hundred times faster than a hard disk, and inside the flash, writing costs far more than reading and erasing more still.

#### A transistor is a switch worked by voltage { #fig-ch0-transistor }

*Figure* · in [§0.6 The transistor as a switch](../core/ch0-foundations.md#06-the-transistor-as-a-switch)

A transistor is a switch worked by voltage: above the threshold voltage, a channel forms and current flows. A flash cell is this device with one change, a charge-storing layer inside the oxide.

#### One read with DMA and an interrupt { #fig-ch0-interrupt-dma }

*Figure* · in [§0.9 Interrupts, polling and DMA](../core/ch0-foundations.md#09-interrupts-polling-and-dma)

The CPU only issues the command and handles the completion; the data moves from the drive into memory without it.

#### A ring buffer { #fig-ch0-ring-buffer }

*Figure* · in [§0.10 Queues and ring buffers](../core/ch0-foundations.md#010-queues-and-ring-buffers)

The producer fills slots at the tail, the consumer empties them at the head, and both wrap around. The entries waiting are those from the head up to the tail.

### [Ch 1 — SSD Overview](../core/ch1-overview.md) { #page-ch1-overview }

#### An HDD reaches data by spinning its platters and swinging an arm { #fig-ch1-hdd-vs-ssd }

*Figure* · in [§1.2 SSD vs HDD](../core/ch1-overview.md#12-ssd-vs-hdd)

An HDD reaches data by spinning its platters and swinging an arm, which costs milliseconds for every random access. An SSD addresses its flash chips electronically in microseconds, and has nothing to break when it is dropped.

The front end speaks the host's protocol; the FTL firmware maps logical addresses to flash, keeping its map in DRAM; the back end corrects errors and drives the flash over parallel channels.

### [Ch 2 — Controllers & AFA](../core/ch2-controllers-afa.md) { #page-ch2-controllers-afa }

#### Inside a controller SoC { #fig-ch2-controller-soc }

*Figure* · in [§2.1 SSD system architecture](../core/ch2-controllers-afa.md#21-ssd-system-architecture)

The dynamic RAM (DRAM) and the NAND flash are separate chips; everything else shares one die. Data moves between the front end, on-chip static RAM (SRAM), the DRAM controller and the back end over the fast AXI bus, while slow peripherals sit on the APB bus.

#### The Flash Timing & Parallelism Lab { #anim-ch2-flash-timing-lab }

*Animation* · in [§2.1.3 Back end (後端)](../core/ch2-controllers-afa.md#213-back-end) · [open the animation page](../animations/flash-timing-lab.md)

Timelines of what the flash bus actually does, drawn to scale with the book's own timings: one shared bus, register pipelining, multi-plane programming and independent plane reads.

#### Channel × die parallelism { #fig-ch2-channels-dies }

*Figure* · in [§2.1.3 Back end (後端)](../core/ch2-controllers-afa.md#213-back-end)

Top: each channel is one shared bus, and its chip-enable (CE#) lines decide which die is listening; at any moment one die per channel is on the bus while others program. Bottom: one channel over time. The bus hands each die its page, then serves the next die while the first one programs. Here a program lasts five transfers, so four dies leave the bus idle between rounds; real program times are many times longer than a page transfer, which is why each channel carries several dies.

#### One 8 KB write through XtremIO's data modules { #fig-ch2-xtremio-write }

*Figure* · in [§2.6.4 Workflow — how IO actually flows](../core/ch2-controllers-afa.md#264-workflow-how-io-actually-flows)

One 8 KB write through XtremIO's data modules (addresses in 4 KB blocks, hashes shortened). Where a block lands depends only on its hash, and a duplicate costs a table update instead of an SSD write.

#### The board around the controller, with M.2's signal names { #fig-ch2-ssd-board }

*Figure* · in [§2.8 The board around the controller](../core/ch2-controllers-afa.md#28-the-board-around-the-controller)

Enterprise drives add the capacitor bank; DRAM-less drives drop the DRAM and borrow host memory instead ([§4.2.3](../core/ch4-ftl.md#423-hmb-host-memory-buffer)).

### [Ch 3 — NAND Flash](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md) { #page-ch3-nand-flash }

#### A flash cell is a transistor with a charge-storage layer between two oxides { #fig-ch3-flash-cell }

*Figure* · in [§3.1.1 How a flash cell works](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#311-how-a-flash-cell-works)

In a floating gate (top) the stored electrons move freely through a conductor, so one weak spot in the tunnel oxide can drain them all; in charge trap (bottom, §3.1.6) each electron stays where it was caught.

#### The Vt Distribution Playground { #anim-ch3-vt-playground }

*Animation* · in [§3.1.2 SLC / MLC / TLC: the threshold-voltage picture](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#312-slc-mlc-tlc-the-threshold-voltage-picture) and [§3.4.2 Read Retry](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#342-read-retry) · [open the animation page](../animations/vt-playground.md)

The threshold-voltage (V<sub>t</sub>) picture behind every Chapter 3 failure mode, made draggable: one cell, then a population of cells, then the bells that wear, retention and reads push into each other.

#### Each bell is the population of cells programmed to one state { #fig-ch3-vt-bells }

*Figure* · in [§3.1.2 SLC / MLC / TLC: the threshold-voltage picture](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#312-slc-mlc-tlc-the-threshold-voltage-picture)

Each bell is the population of cells programmed to one state, spread along the threshold-voltage axis; the dashed lines are the read references a read tests against. Every extra bit per cell doubles the number of bells in the same voltage window, so the shaded margins between neighbours shrink from SLC's wide gap to TLC's slivers.

#### Why SSDs need an FTL — NAND flash, animated { #anim-ch3-nand-flash-animation }

*Animation* · in [§3.1.3 The hierarchy: cell → page → block → plane → die](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#313-the-hierarchy-cell-page-block-plane-die) · [open the animation page](../animations/nand-flash-animation.md)

A guided walk through NAND's physical rules, and the consequences they force: out-of-place writes, garbage collection and write amplification.

#### The hierarchy { #fig-ch3-hierarchy }

*Figure* · in [§3.1.3 The hierarchy: cell → page → block → plane → die](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#313-the-hierarchy-cell-page-block-plane-die)

A die runs commands; its planes each own a page register and a cache register; a plane holds many blocks; and inside a block, the cells along one wordline form a page (three pages in TLC). The block's cells share one substrate, so the block is what an erase clears.

#### The same series string, flat and standing { #fig-ch3-nand-2d-3d }

*Figure* · in [§3.1.5 3D flash](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#315-3d-flash)

In 2D (top) shrinking the cells brought neighbours close enough to interfere; in 3D (bottom) the string runs up a channel hole through the wordline layers, one cell per layer, and the etched hole narrows toward the bottom.

#### The Flash Timing & Parallelism Lab { #anim-ch3-flash-timing-lab }

*Animation* · in [§3.2.5 Read / write / erase on the wire](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#325-read-write-erase-on-the-wire) · [open the animation page](../animations/flash-timing-lab.md)

Timelines of what the flash bus actually does, drawn to scale with the book's own timings: one shared bus, register pipelining, multi-plane programming and independent plane reads.

#### The integrity stack as a ladder { #fig-ch3-integrity-ladder }

*Figure* · in [§3.4 Fighting back: the data-integrity stack](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#34-fighting-back-the-data-integrity-stack)

The integrity stack as a ladder: each rung is costlier and rarer than the one above, and Read Scrub works in the background to keep pages from reaching the lower rungs.

#### The failure modes as bell movements { #fig-ch3-vt-shifts }

*Figure* · in [§3.4.1 Sources of read error, consolidated](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#341-sources-of-read-error-consolidated)

Cells that cross the read reference read wrong (red). After retention or read disturb the bells are still apart, so a shifted reference (Read Retry) reads them correctly; after heavy wear the tails overlap, and only ECC can fix the stragglers.

#### Stronger ECC in action — BCH & LDPC { #anim-ch3-ecc-bch-ldpc }

*Animation* · in [§3.4.3 ECC: error-correcting codes](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#343-ecc-error-correcting-codes) · [open the animation page](../animations/ecc-bch-ldpc.md)

The two codes SSDs actually ship: BCH, which locates errors algebraically, and LDPC, which corrects them by passing messages on a graph.

#### Stripe RAID & the Chained Warships { #anim-ch3-stripe-raid }

*Animation* · in [§3.4.4 RAID inside the SSD](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#344-raid-inside-the-ssd) · [open the animation page](../animations/stripe-raid.md)

Four data dies and one XOR parity die. Losing a die's block is survivable, but the parity ties a stripe's members together.

#### Three answers to "where does the periphery go?" { #fig-ch3-cmos-placement }

*Figure* · in [§3.5.2 Peripheral circuits: beside → under → bonded](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#352-peripheral-circuits-beside-under-bonded)

Three answers to "where does the periphery go?": beside the array, under it, or on a separate wafer bonded to it.

#### WA against OP, computed from two models { #fig-ch4-op-wa }

*Figure* · in [§4.3.2 Write amplification](../core/ch4-ftl.md#432-write-amplification)

The upper curve is this section's worst case, WA = (1 + OP) ÷ OP, through the two worked points. The lower curve models uniform random writes with the oldest block cleaned first (its WA is about 3.2 at 20% OP and 1.7 at 50%); greedy victim choice does better still. *Animation* · in [§4.6 Power-loss recovery](../core/ch4-ftl.md#46-power-loss-recovery) · [open the animation page](../animations/power-loss-rebuild.md)

The map table lives in RAM, and RAM forgets at power-off. This animation shows how the drive rebuilds the map from what every flash page carries with it.

#### Recovery in two moves { #fig-ch4-plr-rebuild }

*Figure* · in [§4.6 Power-loss recovery](../core/ch4-ftl.md#46-power-loss-recovery)

Recovery in two moves: load the last snapshot and rescan only what was written after it; when two pages claim the same LBA, the newer timestamp wins.

#### The SLC cache's signature (schematic) { #fig-ch4-slc-cache }

*Figure* · in [§4.8 SLC cache](../core/ch4-ftl.md#48-slc-cache)

The SLC cache's signature (schematic): burst speed until the cache fills, then the native cells' speed. In idle time the drive folds the cached data into its native triple-level (TLC) or quad-level (QLC) cells and frees the cache again.

### [Supp A — ECC Coding Theory](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md) { #page-a-ecc-coding-theory }

#### The communication-system model { #fig-a-channel-model }

*Figure* · in [§A.2 The communication-system model](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md#a2-the-communication-system-model)

The communication-system model, traced with the Hamming(7,4) example of §A.3.3. The encoder adds structure, the channel adds an error, and the decoder uses the structure to find the error and remove it.

#### How ECC finds and fixes a bit — Hamming visualizer { #anim-a-ecc-bit-correction }

*Animation* · in [§A.3.2 Parity: the cornerstone](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md#a32-parity-the-cornerstone) · [open the animation page](../animations/ecc-bit-correction.md)

A Hamming(12,8) code at work: flip a bit, and the parity checks that fail spell out its position.

#### The example's Tanner graph: one edge for every 1 in H { #fig-a-tanner-graph }

*Figure* · in [§A.4.2 The Tanner graph](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md#a42-the-tanner-graph)

Each bit sits in two checks and each check ties three bits; decoding sends messages back and forth along these twelve edges.

#### Stronger ECC in action — BCH & LDPC { #anim-a-ecc-bch-ldpc }

*Animation* · in [§A.5 LDPC decoding](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md#a5-ldpc-decoding) · [open the animation page](../animations/ecc-bch-ldpc.md)

The two codes SSDs actually ship: BCH, which locates errors algebraically, and LDPC, which corrects them by passing messages on a graph.

#### What extra strobes buy { #fig-a-soft-read }

*Figure* · in [§A.7 The LDPC codec inside the SSD](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md#a7-the-ldpc-codec-inside-the-ssd)

A hard read sorts cells only by side, so a misread cell near the reference (red) gets the same confident ±4 as a cell far from it. Five strobes split the axis into six bins, and the LLRs, computed here from the two bells drawn, fall to ±1 near the reference: the decoder learns which bits to doubt.

#### The escalation ladder { #fig-a-decode-ladder }

*Figure* · in [§A.7 The LDPC codec inside the SSD](../supplements/a-ecc-coding-theory.md#a7-the-ldpc-codec-inside-the-ssd)

A read moves down a rung only when decoding fails and stops at the first rung that succeeds, so nearly every read ends on rung 1. Rung 4 is the die-level RAID of [Ch 3 §3.4.4](../core/ch3-nand-flash.md#344-raid-inside-the-ssd); the bottom is the UBER event of [Ch 1 §1.5.4](../core/ch1-overview.md#154-data-reliability).

### [Supp B — UFS](../supplements/b-ufs.md) { #page-b-ufs }

#### The UFS stack beside its PCIe/NVMe counterparts { #fig-b-ufs-stack }

*Figure* · in [§B.2 The UFS protocol stack](../supplements/b-ufs.md#b2-the-ufs-protocol-stack)

Host and device each run the whole stack; only the physical lanes join them.

#### One random read with and without HPB, not to scale { #fig-b-hpb }

*Figure* · in [§B.8 HPB: Host Performance Booster](../supplements/b-ufs.md#b8-hpb-host-performance-booster)

On a map-cache miss the device must read its map from flash before the data; with HPB the host's lookup in its own memory takes a fraction of a microsecond and removes that first flash read.

### [Supp C — Flash File Systems](../supplements/c-flash-file-systems.md) { #page-c-flash-file-systems }

#### An EXT4 volume is a row of block groups { #fig-c-ext4-layout }

*Figure* · in [§C.1.2 On-disk structure](../supplements/c-flash-file-systems.md#c12-on-disk-structure)

An EXT4 volume is a row of block groups, and every group carries its own bookkeeping ahead of its data, so a file's metadata can sit near its blocks: a seek-saving layout from the disk era.

#### The six F2FS areas { #fig-c-f2fs-layout }

*Figure* · in [§C.2.1 Disk layout](../supplements/c-flash-file-systems.md#c21-disk-layout)

The five on the left are metadata, updated in place; the main area is append-only. In green, each structure's twin inside the drive's FTL.

#### Log-on-log { #fig-c-log-on-log }

*Figure* · in [§C.2.5 The log-on-log problem — and the ZNS fix](../supplements/c-flash-file-systems.md#c25-the-log-on-log-problem-and-the-zns-fix)

On a conventional SSD two logs are stacked, each with its own map and its own collector, and their write amplification multiplies; on a zoned device F2FS's log is the only one.

### [Supp D — Power Management](../supplements/d-power-management.md) { #page-d-power-management }

#### The five layers of power management { #fig-d-power-layers }

*Figure* · in [Supplement D — SSD Power Management](../supplements/d-power-management.md#supplement-d-ssd-power-management)

The five layers of power management, from the host's system states down to the sideband pins. Each layer has its own states and its own driver, and the drive reaches its idle floor only when every layer is down.

#### The link ladder as a trade-off, not to scale { #fig-d-link-ladder }

*Figure* · in [§D.1 PCIe link power states & ASPM](../supplements/d-power-management.md#d1-pcie-link-power-states-aspm)

The link ladder as a trade-off, not to scale: each step to the right draws less power while idle and takes longer to wake.

#### One idle period, not to scale { #fig-d-apst-timeline }

*Figure* · in [§D.3 NVMe power states & APST](../supplements/d-power-management.md#d3-nvme-power-states-apst)

The link parks within moments of the last I/O; the controller descends in steps, after idle times the host configured; and the deepest state costs the longest climb back when I/O returns.

### [Supp E — Aerospace Storage](../supplements/e-aerospace-storage.md) { #page-e-aerospace-storage }

#### Radiation's two kinds of damage { #fig-e-radiation-effects }

*Figure* · in [§E.2 Radiation effects & mitigation](../supplements/e-aerospace-storage.md#e2-radiation-effects-mitigation)

The slow kind ages the chip the way wear does; the instant kind ranges from a flipped bit to a dead chip, and each tier calls for a different defence.

#### Where a die is tough and where it is soft { #fig-e-nand-soft-spots }

*Figure* · in [§E.2.3 Where NAND is tough, and where it's soft](../supplements/e-aerospace-storage.md#e23-where-nand-is-tough-and-where-its-soft)

The array's large stored charge shrugs off most strikes; the periphery that runs it takes the damage, from upsets and hangs to destruction at the high-voltage pumps.

### [Supp F — Security & Sanitization](../supplements/f-security.md) { #page-f-security }

#### The SED key hierarchy { #fig-f-sed-keys }

*Figure* · in [§F.2 Self-encrypting drives](../supplements/f-security.md#f2-self-encrypting-drives)

Only a wrapped copy of the media key is ever stored, and the key that unwraps it exists only while the right password is supplied. Destroying the media key makes every block unreadable at once.

#### Where copies of data live inside an SSD { #fig-f-erase-scope }

*Figure* · in [§F.4.1 Delete, Trim and overwrite](../supplements/f-security.md#f41-delete-trim-and-overwrite)

Host-level deletion touches only what the host can address; only commands that work inside the drive reach the rest.

#### The chain of trust { #fig-f-boot-chain }

*Figure* · in [§F.5 Secure boot and signed firmware](../supplements/f-security.md#f5-secure-boot-and-signed-firmware)

Each stage verifies the next before running it, starting from code that can't be changed; the fuses anchor both the vendor's key and the oldest version the drive will accept.

### [Supp G — Firmware: Boot, Update & Debug](../supplements/g-firmware.md) { #page-g-firmware }

#### An SSD's boot { #fig-g-boot-sequence }

*Figure* · in [§G.2 Boot: from power-on to ready](../supplements/g-firmware.md#g2-boot-from-power-on-to-ready)

Each stage loads and checks the next, every stage has a fallback copy, and the drive reports ready only once its mapping table is usable.

#### A firmware update through slots { #fig-g-fw-slots }

*Figure* · in [§G.3 Updating firmware in the field](../supplements/g-firmware.md#g3-updating-firmware-in-the-field)

The new image is checked before it is written, written before it is activated, and the old images stay where they are until the new one has proved itself.

#### The field-return loop { #fig-g-rma-loop }

*Figure* · in [§G.6 From the factory to the field](../supplements/g-firmware.md#g6-from-the-factory-to-the-field)

Every turn of it fixes a whole population of drives, not just the one returned, as long as the evidence of step 2 exists.

### [Supp H — The Host Side: OS Stack & Tools](../supplements/h-host-stack.md) { #page-h-host-stack }

#### One read through the Linux storage stack { #fig-h-io-path }

*Figure* · in [§H.1 One read, traced](../supplements/h-host-stack.md#h1-one-read-traced)

Everything above the drive is software on the host's processor; the layers exist so that any filesystem works with any drive.

#### One queue pair per core { #fig-h-queue-mapping }

*Figure* · in [§H.2 Queues per core](../supplements/h-host-stack.md#h2-queues-per-core)

A core submits and completes entirely on its own queues, and the completion's interrupt is steered back to the same core, so no two cores ever contend for a queue.

### [Supp I — Data-Center SSDs](../supplements/i-data-center.md) { #page-i-data-center }

#### Read latency by percentile, illustrative values { #fig-i-tail-latency }

*Figure* · in [§I.1 What data centers want: consistent latency](../supplements/i-data-center.md#i1-what-data-centers-want-consistent-latency)

The median looks excellent; the tail is what a large service actually feels.

#### Data-center SSD form factors, to scale { #fig-i-form-factors-dc }

*Figure* · in [§I.2 Form factors: U.2, U.3 and EDSFF](../supplements/i-data-center.md#i2-form-factors-u2-u3-and-edsff)

Each EDSFF shape trades length, width and thickness for capacity, power and cooling; the E1.L ruler fills the depth of a server.

#### A dual-port SSD { #fig-i-dual-port }

*Figure* · in [§I.5 Dual port, multipath and ANA](../supplements/i-data-center.md#i5-dual-port-multipath-and-ana)

Both hosts see the same namespace; the drive tells them which path to prefer, and the other path is ready if the first one fails.
